problems.title: Basic Concepts
problems.statement: It is a common misunderstanding that oil is located in the form of an underground lake. Actually, it is found in very small pores with a size comparable to the diameter of human hair. Void space between particles of sand is filled with oil like a sponge is filled with water. If one pushes on the sponge, water comes out. A similar thing occurs with oilsaturated rocks, which are located a few kilometers beneath the surface of the Earth. When all the rocks above the reservoir exert a huge pressure on the petroleum sponge, the oil flows to the surface (see Figure 1). In this problem we neglect capillary and gravity effects on the fluid flow.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Scheme of the oil production process
figures.alt: Cross-section of the ground: a drilling derrick on the surface, a yellow well going down through brown rock layers and branching horizontally at the bottom in a dark reservoir layer. Labels: WELL (hole to the surface), IMPERMEABLE ROCKS, RESERVOIR (porous medium filled with oil).

figures.caption: Figure 2: Representation of the porous medium (grains in white and void space in blue)
figures.alt: A cube of porous rock: white dotted grains packed together with blue void space between them.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Cubic stacking of identical spherical grains
figures.alt: Eight identical grey spheres stacked in a simple cubic arrangement, two layers of four.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Schematic of the viscous fluid flow in the tube.
figures.alt: A horizontal tube of length L_0 filled with molecules (black dots with arrows); pressure P_1 at the left end and P_2 at the right end; in the middle a parabolic velocity profile v with blue arrows and the radial coordinate y measured from the axis.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Diagram showing definition of Darcy’s law
figures.alt: A rectangular rock sample of length L and cross-section A with inlet pressure P_in and flow q on the left and outlet pressure P_out on the right; a small region is magnified into a cube of rock, which is further shown as a cylinder containing a twisted capillary tube.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Composite rock sample

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement:
One of the most important characteristics of the reservoir is porosity, which is the fraction of the void space in the rock to the total volume:

$$\varphi = \frac{V_{void}}{V_{grains} + V_{void}}\ ,\tag{1}$$

where $V$ stands for the volume.

To understand meaning of this concept, imagine identical balls (grains of sand) that put in a pile as shown in Figure 3.

Find the porosity of the system if the number of balls is infinitely large.

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement:
A fluid flow between the grains of sand is controlled by viscosity and permeability. Consider a flow of the viscous fluid through a tube with length $L_0$ and radius $r_0$ (Figure 4). Fluid molecules moves along free paths and collide with each other. However, this process is not uniform. Close to the solid boundary molecules are stuck, while in other regions velocity varies, with a profile similar to the sketch shown in Figure 4, where $y$ is measured from the axis of the tube.

The reason for this effect is the internal friction of the fluid, or viscosity. If two adjacent layers of fluid flow with slightly different speeds, the random sidewise intrusion of some faster molecules into the slower stream will tend to speed up the slower stream, whereas intrusion of slower molecules into the faster stream will tend to slow down the faster stream. This effect could be quantified with following well-known equation:

$$F_{fr} = -\mu A_{fr}\frac{dv}{dy}\ ,\tag{2}$$

where $F_{fr}$ is a friction force which occurs between two thin layers of the fluid separated by a small distance $dy$, which have differences in velocities $dv$; $A_{fr}$ is a contact area on which applied the internal friction force; $\mu$ is the fluid property called coefficient of viscosity.

Find the velocity distribution $v(y)$ in terms of $\mu$, $L_0$, $r_0$, $P_1$ and $P_2$ . Assume that a mean free path of molecules is much smaller than the radius of the tube.

parts.label: (c)
parts.statement:
Under described conditions fluid will flow through the tube with a flow rate:

$$q = \frac{k_0}{\mu}\pi r_0^2\frac{P_1 - P_2}{L_0}. \qquad \textit{(Poiseuille equation)}\tag{3}$$

Calculate coefficient $k_0$ in Poiseuille equation.

parts.label: (d)
parts.statement:
A fluid flow through a porous medium is governed by Darcy’s law:

$$q = \frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{k}{\mu}A\frac{(P_{in} - P_{out})}{L}\ ,\tag{4}$$

where $\frac{dV}{dt}$ is the amount of fluid transferred through the rock in some period of time; $A, L$ are the cross-sectional area and length of the sample shown in Figure 5; $P_{in} - P_{out}$ is the pressure drop; $k$ is the permeability and is the property of the rock

(*You can easily recognize some similarity with Fouriers Law for heat transfer. Using analogies with heat transfer could significantly help in solution of this problem, because approaches are very similar*).

Porous medium can be modeled as a system of twisted tubes (Figure 5), with permeability $k = k_0\varphi^2$ Where $k_0$ is permeability of a straight capillary; $\varphi^2$ accounts for nonlinearity of the tubes in a porous medium with porosity $\varphi$.

Estimate permeability of the system described in 1.a, with radiuses of the balls equal to $10^{-6}$ m.

parts.label: (e)
parts.statement:
Usually, rock properties are not uniform throughout the reservoir. However, it is possible to apply an averaging procedure to find an effective permeability $k_{eff}$. This means that the initial system could be replaced with a new model that has the same sizes and fluid flow parameters with the only difference in permeability, which is uniform throughout the new homogeneous sample. To examine this issue, we consider a sample consisting of two different rock types as shown in Figure 6. An incompressible fluid flows through that system with a flow rate $q$ and viscosity $\mu$.

Calculate pressure at the boundary between two different rocks $P_b$ in terms of $q$, $\mu$, and parameters shown in Figure 6.

parts.label: (f)
parts.statement: Find the effective permeability of the system $k_{eff}$.

solution.statement:
**1.1** Let’s cut a cube from the pile of balls, as shown in figure on the right. Using definition of porosity:

$$\varphi = \frac{(2r)^3 - 8\cdot\frac{1}{8}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right)}{(2r)^3} = 1 - \frac{\pi}{6}$$

$$\boxed{\varphi = 0.476\ \ or\ \ 47.6\%}$$

**1.2** If fluid is incompressible, fluid velocity along the tube is constant. It varies in the radial direction only, what is due to viscous forces. Let’s consider a part of the fluid with a cylindrical shape, with radius $y$, which is coaxial to the cylinder with radius $r_0$. Using definition of the internal friction, force balance could be written in the following way:

$$(p_1 - p_2)\cdot\pi y^2 = -2\pi y L_0\mu\frac{dv}{dy}\tag{1.2.1}$$

After rearranging variables

$$\frac{(p_1 - p_2)}{2\mu L_0}\int_{r_0}^{y} y dy = -\int_0^{v} dv$$

which results in velocity distribution:

$$\boxed{v(y) = \frac{(p_1 - p_2)}{4\mu L_0}(r_0^2 - y^2)}\tag{1.2.2}$$

**1.3** Total fluid volume, flowing through the tube in a unit of time:

$$q = \int_0^{r_0} v * 2\pi y dy = \frac{(p_1 - p_2)\pi}{2\mu L_0}\int_0^{r_0}(r_0^2 y - y^3)dy = \frac{(p_1 - p_2)\pi r_0^4}{8\mu L_0}\tag{1.3.1}$$

Comparing with Poiseuille equation

$$\boxed{k_0 = \frac{r_0^2}{8}}\tag{1.3.2}$$

**1.4** For estimations one can assume that porous medium could be modeled as tubes with the radiuses equal to the size of balls:

$$k \approx \frac{r_0^2}{8}\left(1 - \frac{\pi}{6}\right)^2\tag{1.4.1}$$

$$\boxed{k \approx 3\cdot 10^{-14}\ m^2}$$

**1.5** From law of conservation of mass and the condition that fluid is incompressible can be concluded that flow rate is constant everywhere:

$$q = \frac{k_1}{\mu}A\frac{P_{in} - P_b}{L_1} = \frac{k_2}{\mu}A\frac{P_b - P_{out}}{L_2}$$

$$\boxed{P_b = \frac{\frac{k_1}{L_1}P_{in} + \frac{k_2}{L_2}P_{out}}{\frac{k_1}{L_1} + \frac{k_2}{L_2}}}\tag{1.5.1}$$

**1.6** Using Eq. (1.5.1)

$$q = \frac{k_{eff}}{\mu}A\frac{P_{in} - P_{out}}{L_1 + L_2} = \frac{A}{\mu}\frac{k_1}{L_1}\left[P_{in} - \frac{\frac{k_1}{L_1}P_{in} + \frac{k_2}{L_2}P_{out}}{\frac{k_1}{L_1} + \frac{k_2}{L_2}}\right]$$

$$\boxed{k_{eff} = \frac{k_1 k_2 (L_1 + L_2)}{k_1 L_2 + k_2 L_1}}\tag{1.6.1}$$

figures.alt: A cube of side 2r cut from the cubic packing of balls: each corner holds one eighth of a ball; the side is marked r and r.

problems.title: Vertical Well
problems.statement: Often the reservoir can be modeled as a cylinder (see Figure 7). For this problem all properties were averaged out as in the previous part, so the reservoir is assumed homogeneous with uniform permeability $k$. Oil can be viewed as an incompressible fluid with viscosity $\mu$. Because the rocks above and below the reservoir are impermeable and the height of the cylinder is much less than its radius ($h \ll R$), one can conclude that the fluid flows only in the radial direction.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Cylindrical reservoir with a vertical well drilled in the center
figures.alt: A flat cylindrical reservoir of radius R=1000 m and height h=10 m with a vertical well of radius r_w=0.1 m drilled in the center; pressure P_b at the outer boundary and P_w at the bottom of the well.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: Find the velocity of the oil $v_w$ inside the well with radius $r_w = 0.1$ m, if the flow rate is 30 $\frac{m^3}{day}$. Estimate the fluid velocity in the reservoir near the well $v_r$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement:
The calculated fluid velocity in the reservoir is rather small therefore the reservoir pressure can be treated as a constant for several months or even years, especially if the reservoir is connected with an underground source of water. Let $P_b$ be the pressure at the outer boundary of the reservoir and $P_w$ be the pressure at the bottom of the well. In this part assume that both $P_b$ and $P_w$ are constants (time-independent values), as well as the radial pressure distribution.

Calculate pressure drop $P_b - P_w$ , which is required to produce oil with flow rate $q$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.statement: Make a sketch of pressure distribution in the reservoir $P(r)$ as a function of the distance from the well.

solution.statement:
**2.1**

$$v_w = \frac{q}{\pi r_w^2} = \frac{30/86400}{3.14\cdot 0.1^2} = 1.1\cdot 10^{-2}\ \frac{m}{sec}$$

$$v_{res} = \frac{q}{2\pi r_w h} = \frac{30/86400}{2\cdot 3.14\cdot 0.1\cdot 10} = 5.5\cdot 10^{-5}\ \frac{m}{sec}$$

Velocity at the reservoir is very small, however it depends on the definition of the fluid velocity in the reservoir. Actually fluid particles moves a few orders of magnitude faster than Darcy’s velocity $\approx \frac{v_{res}}{\varphi}$.

**2.2** For incompressible fluid

$$q = \frac{k}{\mu}2\pi rh\frac{dP}{dr} = const\tag{2.2.1}$$

Rearranging variables

$$\int_{P_w}^{P} dP = \frac{q\mu}{2\pi kh}\int_{r_w}^{r}\frac{dr}{r}$$

$$P - P_w = \frac{q\mu}{2\pi kh}ln\left(\frac{r}{r_w}\right)\tag{2.2.2}$$

Finally

$$\boxed{P_b - P_w = \frac{q\mu}{2\pi kh}ln\left(\frac{R}{r_w}\right)}\tag{2.2.3}$$

**2.3**

figures.alt: Sketch of pressure versus radius across the reservoir cross-section of height h: the pressure curve is lowest (P_w) at the well r_w in the middle and rises logarithmically towards P_b at the boundaries R on both sides; a dashed line marks the average pressure p̄; an arrow labelled q = constant points up the well; axes labelled Pressure and r.

problems.title: Modeling Reservoir Depletion
problems.statement:
In this part the depletion process will be analyzed for the reservoir shown in Figure 8. The well has a horizontal part, therefore, the fluid flow in the reservoir is linear ($h \ll L$).

This time, pressure at the bottom of the well $P_w$ is constant (hydrostatic column of oil). However, the pressure at the boundary $P_b(t)$ is changing with time, as well as the oil production rate $q(t)$. In this model the flow rate of the fluid is given by:

$$q = -2\varphi L^2 c_r h\frac{d\bar{P}}{dt}\ ,\tag{5}$$

where $c_r$ is the compressibility of the rock, and the average pressure inside the reservoir $\bar{P}$ is approximated by:

$$\bar{P} \approx \frac{P_b + P_w}{2}.\tag{6}$$

figures.caption: Figure 8: System used for modeling reservoir depletion
figures.alt: A flat rectangular reservoir of height h, width L and length 2L (two halves of length L) with a well descending into its center, where the pressure is P_w; pressure P_b at both end faces; blue arrows show flow from both ends towards the well.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: Derive an explicit expression for $q(t)$ in terms of $k, \mu, c_r, \varphi$ and reservoir dimensions, if the initial flow rate is $q_0$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement: For the system described in this section, determine the time needed to deplete the oil reservoir by a half.

parts.label: (c)
parts.statement: Historically, first attempts to predict reservoir performance were made by doing analogies to electric circuits. Draw a simple electric circuit, which is analogous to the system described in Part 3.

answer.value: A circuit with a capacitor and a resistor (RC circuit).

parts.label: (d)
parts.statement:
The reason why gas reservoirs cannot be modeled with the circuit as in 3.c, is that gas is highly compressible, with a compressibility being strongly dependent on the applied pressure. Compressibility is defined as:

$$c = -\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{dV}{dP}\right)_T\ ,\tag{7}$$

where $V$ is initial volume of the examined sample, $dV$ is isothermal volume change, when additional pressure $dP$ is applied.

Assuming natural gas as ideal, derive its compressibility $c_g$ as function of pressure $P$.

solution.statement:
**3.1**

$$q = \frac{dV_{fluid}}{dt} = \frac{d(\varphi V_{res})}{dt} = \varphi V_{res}\left(\frac{1}{V_{res}}\frac{dV_{res}}{d\bar{p}}\right)\frac{d\bar{p}}{dt} = -2\varphi L^2 hc_r\frac{d\bar{p}}{dt}$$

$$\boxed{\alpha = -2\varphi L^2 hc_r}\tag{3.1.1}$$

**3.2** Applying Darcy’s law:

$$q = 2\frac{k}{\mu}Lh\frac{P_b - P_w}{L} = -2\varphi L^2 hc_r\frac{d\bar{p}}{dt}\tag{3.2.1}$$

Average pressure can be estimated as:

$$\bar{p} \approx \frac{P_b + P_w}{2}\tag{3.2.2}$$

Considering that $P_w$ is constant:

$$d\bar{p} \approx \frac{1}{2}dP_b\tag{3.2.3}$$

Solving Eq.(3.2.3) and (3.2.1)

$$\int_{P_b(0)}^{P_b(t)}\frac{dP_b}{P_b - P_w} = -\frac{2k}{\mu L^2 c_r\varphi}\int_0^{t} dt$$

$$ln\left(\frac{P_b(t) - P_w}{P_b(t) - P_w}\right) = -\frac{2k}{\mu L^2 c_r\varphi}t$$

Using definition of the flow rate from Eq. (3.2.1)

$$ln\left(\frac{q(t)}{q_0}\right) = -\frac{2k}{\mu L^2 c_r\varphi}t$$

$$\boxed{q(t) = q_o exp\left(-\frac{2k}{\mu L^2 c_r\varphi}t\right)}\tag{3.2.4}$$

**3.3**

$$V_{produced} = \int_o^T q(t)dt\tag{3.3.1}$$

Using Eq. (3.2.4)

$$V_{produced} = -\frac{\mu L^2 c_r\varphi}{2k}q_o exp\left(-\frac{2k}{\mu L^2 c_r\varphi}t\right)\Big|_o^T = \frac{\mu L^2 c_r\varphi}{2k}q_o\left[1 - exp\left(-\frac{2k}{\mu L^2 c_r\varphi}T\right)\right]\tag{3.3.2}$$

From the problem statement, volume of oil produced is a half of the initial reserves:

$$V_{produced} = \frac{1}{2}V_{res}\varphi = \frac{1}{2}(2L^2 h)\varphi\tag{3.3.3}$$

Thus

$$\boxed{T = \frac{\mu L^2 c_r\varphi}{2k}ln\left(\frac{1}{1 - \frac{2kh}{\mu c_r q_0}}\right)}\tag{3.3.4}$$

Equation (3.3.4) gives rather bad results for real data, because the fluid flow model was very rough, nevertheless order of the magnitude usually is very close to the results from numerical simulations.

**3.4** Equation for the flow rate $\boldsymbol{q(t)}$ derived in the part 3.2 is an exponential decline. Similar equation could be obtained for the circuit with a capacitor and a resistor. There a flow rate is analogous to the charge at the capacitor plate and term with compressibility is analogous to the resistor.

**3.5** Ideal gas law:

$$V = \frac{\vartheta RT}{P}\tag{3.5.1}$$

Differentiating Eq. (3.5.1)

$$\left(\frac{dV}{dP}\right)_T = -\frac{1}{p^2}\vartheta RT\tag{3.5.2}$$

Using definition of the compressibility and Eq. (3.5.2) results in

$$\boxed{c_g = -\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{dV}{dP}\right)_T = \frac{1}{p}}\tag{3.5.3}$$

As it is seen with higher pressure gas behaves more like a fluid, with negligible compressibility. However during production, when pressure drops significantly, gas production deviates from exponential decline.

figures.alt: A simple closed circuit consisting of a capacitor (top) and a resistor (bottom) connected in a loop.

problems.title: Fractured Reservoir
problems.statement:
Most of the world’s largest oil reservoirs have a different structure, which is not a pile of small balls with fluid between, but a very complex system of porous medium and fractures as shown in Figure 9 (left). Fortunately, such reservoirs could be easily modeled with a stack of sugar cubes, as in Figure 9 (right).

In the model supposed that the production from fractured reservoir goes from the matrix to the fracture and therefrom to the well. Thus, matrix does not produce directly into the well. Such a simple model gives incredibly good results for oil production forecasts with an equation:

$$q = \sigma\frac{a^3}{\mu}(P_m - P_f)\ ,\tag{8}$$

where $q$ is a flow rate from matrix to fracture, $P_m$ is average pressure at the matrix, $P_f$ is pressure at fracture, near the boundary of the sugar cube with a side $a$, and $\sigma$ is shape factor, related to the dimensions of the sugar cubes.

The goal of this part of the problem is to estimate shape factor $\sigma$. Consider a cube with the side $a$ filled with a porous medium with porosity $\varphi$, permeability $k$, and compressibility $c_r$. Oil flows with a constant rate $q$ symmetrically from the center of the cube to its boundaries, where pressure is equal $P_f$, which changes with time $t$. Furthermore, if the well producing at constant flow rate then the cell pressure will decline in such a way that

$$\frac{dP_m}{dt} \approx \text{ const for all } x \text{ and } t.\tag{9}$$

figures.caption: Figure 9: Cubic stacking of identical spherical grains
figures.alt: Two drawings side by side. Left, ACTUAL RESERVOIR: a block of rock (Matrix) cut by irregular dark fractures (Fracture). Right, MODEL RESERVOIR: a regular stack of small cubes (Matrix block) separated by fractures (Fracture).

figures.caption: Figure 10: Cubic stacking of identical spherical grains
figures.alt: Cross-section of one matrix cube surrounded by a hatched fracture (label Fracture); an inner square marks the surface where the pressure is p_m(x); arrows from the center show the distance x to the inner square and a/2 to the cube boundary.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: Calculate pressure distribution inside the cube $P_m(x)$ in terms of $P_f, a, \mu, k,$ and, $q$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement: What is the shape factor for the cube with side $a$ ?

solution.statement:
**4.1** At first let’s find the constant for pressure decline. The condition $\frac{dp_m}{dt} = const$ allows to write the following:

$$q = \frac{dV_{fluid}}{dt} = V_{fluid}\left(\frac{1}{V_{fluid}}\frac{dV_{fluid}}{dp_m}\right)\frac{dp_m}{dt} = -a^3\varphi c_r\frac{dp_m}{dt}$$

Or

$$\frac{dp_m}{dt} = -\frac{q}{a^3\varphi c_r} = const\tag{4.1.1}$$

Material balance equation for the thin layer, shown in figure above:

$$v(x)A(x) - v(x + dx)A(x + dx) = \frac{dV}{dt}\tag{4.1.2}$$

A – stands for area; V – is volume of the analyzed thin layer with thickness dx. Using definition of compressibility, Eq. (4.1.2) can be simplified as

$$d(vA) = [6\cdot(2x)^2 dx]\cdot c_r\varphi\frac{dp_m}{dt}\tag{4.1.3}$$

Using Eq. (4.1.1) and Darcy’s law, Eq. (4.1.3) can be rewritten as

$$d\left(\frac{k}{\mu}\frac{dp_m}{dx}6\cdot(2x)^2\right) = -[6\cdot(2x)^2 dx]\cdot\frac{q}{a^3}\tag{4.1.4}$$

$$\int d\left(x^2\frac{dp_m}{dx}\right) = -\frac{\mu}{k}\frac{q}{a^3}\int x^2 dx$$

$$x^2\frac{dp_m}{dx} = -\frac{\mu}{k}\frac{q}{a^3}\frac{x^3}{3} + C_1$$

where $C_1$ is some constant

$$\frac{dp_m}{dx} = -\frac{\mu}{k}\frac{q}{a^3}\frac{x}{3} + \frac{C_1}{x^2}\tag{4.1.5}$$

Eq. (4.1.5) will have meaning for the center of the cube ($x = 0$) only if $C_1 = 0$, otherwise pressure gradient $\frac{dp_m}{dx}$, which corresponds to the velocity in the center of the cube, will be infinite, what is meaningless from the point of physics. Thus,

$$\frac{dp_m}{dx} = -\frac{\mu}{3k}\frac{q}{a^3}x\tag{4.1.6}$$

Integrating one more time

$$\int_{p_f}^{p_m(x)} dp_m = -\frac{\mu}{3k}\frac{q}{a^3}\int_{a/2}^{x} xdx$$

$$\boxed{p_m(x) = p_f + \frac{\mu}{6k}\frac{q}{a^3}\left(\frac{a^2}{4} - x^2\right)}\tag{4.1.7}$$

**4.2** Calculate average pressure in the matrix with using Eq.(4.1.7)

$$\bar{p}_m = \frac{\int_0^{a/2} p_m(x)\cdot 6\cdot(2x)^2 dx}{a^3} = p_f + \frac{\mu q}{60ka}\tag{4.2.1}$$

Definition of the shape factor:

$$\sigma = \frac{q\mu}{ka^3(\bar{p}_m - p_f)}\tag{4.2.2}$$

Substituting Eq. (4.2.1) into (4.2.2) results in

$$\sigma = \frac{60}{a^2}\tag{4.2.3}$$

figures.alt: Cross-section of the matrix cube inside the hatched fracture (label Fracture); a thin square layer of thickness dx at distance x from the center, with velocities v(x) and v(x + dx) marked by arrows at its inner and outer faces.
